reasoning: The underlying problem — detecting APPS backdoors and building cost-efficient layered defenses — is heavily studied in the AI control literature (Greenblatt et al. 2023; Control Tax 2506.05296; cost-constrained monitor stacking 2507.15886), and individual components of the proposal already exist: differential/fuzz testing against a reference is the standard mechanism used to *define and confirm* APPS backdoors (an input where candidate diverges from reference), and the "suspicious constructs" (rare magic constants, standalone conditionals) are exactly what LLM monitors are prompted to flag. However, this work uniformly treats the LLM monitor as the detector and deterministic test-running as part of the backdoor definition; no study I found explicitly characterizes the standalone catch rate of a purely deterministic, non-AI validator stack (diff testing + lint + complexity) as a defensive layer with its own ROC, nor ablates how stacking it in front of a cheap LLM monitor changes total detection and answers "when is an LLM monitor even needed." A methodological caveat: differential testing presumes access to a trusted reference solution, which is not available at deployment in the realistic AI control threat model — this weakens the framing's validity but does not change the novelty verdict. The specific combination/angle is unexplored, so partially_addressed rather than largely_addressed.

evidence.title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion (Greenblatt et al., 2023)
evidence.summary: Foundational AI control paper defining the APPS backdoor setting: untrusted model inserts a backdoor that passes all unit tests but produces wrong output on a red-team-submitted exploit input. Blue-team protocol decisions (audit/defer/run) rely on an LLM trusted monitor's suspicion score; differential execution vs a reference is used to define/confirm backdoors, not as a standalone measured defensive layer.

evidence.title: Control Tax: The Price of Keeping AI in Check
evidence.summary: Uses the APPS backdoor red-teaming setting and systematically measures LLM monitor ROC/detection rate vs cost across many models, translating ROC curves into deployment safety. Focuses entirely on LLM monitors as detectors; does not characterize a deterministic non-AI validator baseline or its standalone catch rate.

evidence.title: Combining Cost-Constrained Runtime Monitors for AI Safety
evidence.summary: Directly studies stacking and combining monitors under cost constraints, showing likelihood-ratio policies and stochastic monitor calls outperform always-on monitoring by trading off spend. Closest prior work to the proposal's stacking question, but frames monitors generically rather than measuring a deterministic-only layer (diff testing/lint/complexity) feeding a cheap LLM.

evidence.title: AutoSafeCoder: A Multi-Agent Framework for Securing LLM Code Generation through Static Analysis and Fuzz Testing
evidence.summary: Combines static analysis and fuzz/differential testing to secure LLM-generated code, showing these deterministic techniques are already applied to AI-generated code vulnerabilities. Demonstrates the component methods exist, though not benchmarked as standalone backdoor-catch-rate baselines in the AI control APPS setting.

evidence.title: Vulnerability in Trusted Monitoring and Mitigations
evidence.summary: Community discussion enumerating suspicious code traits LLM monitors key on (standalone conditionals, conditional checks unrelated to functionality, special-case comments) — exactly the constructs the proposal's static lint validator would target, indicating the signal is known but typically delegated to the LLM monitor rather than a deterministic linter.

evidence.title: When is an LLM monitor needed / monitor performance influence (Adaptive Attacks on Trusted Monitors Subvert AI Control Protocols)
evidence.summary: Examines how monitor strength influences AI control protocol safety, noting the precise influence of monitor performance remains poorly understood. Confirms the field's open question about monitor necessity/strength, but addresses it via LLM monitors and adaptive attacks rather than via a deterministic-vs-LLM standalone comparison.
